what: A client-side rendered single-page app (CSR SPA) ships one near-empty HTML file plus JavaScript bundles. The browser runs the JavaScript, which fetches data, builds the page and handles every later navigation without a full reload.
like: Like a flat-pack wardrobe: the box (HTML) arrives nearly empty, and you build everything at home (in the browser) from the parts inside.
why: Cheapest hosting - plain static files on a CDN, no render server
App-like feel after the first load: no full reloads, state survives navigation
Great fit for logged-in tools and dashboards where SEO does not matter

steps.d: The browser asks for any URL and the host returns the same small index.html with an empty root div and script tags. This is why one file serves every route.
The bundle (framework, router, your code) downloads, parses and executes. Nothing meaningful is visible until this finishes, so the first paint is usually a blank page or spinner.
Only now does the app know which route it is on and call the API. This creates a waterfall: HTML, then JS, then data, then render.
The app renders into the DOM. Since the same code that drew the page also owns the handlers, it is interactive straight away - no hydration step.
Later clicks swap views in place using the History API and fetch just the new data. Code splitting loads only the route chunk that is needed.

numbers.l: suggested budget for critical-path resources (compressed) for slow networks and cheap devices
good LCP and INP thresholds, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads
rough TTFB guide; for SPAs a fast first byte matters because rendering cannot start before the JS arrives

choices.t: Pure SPA or a framework with CSR mode
choices.d: A pure SPA (Vite + React) is simplest to host. Next.js can also start as a strict SPA or static export and add server features later, so the choice is reversible.

Start fetches as early as possible - in the route loader or a server-provided promise - instead of inside components after render. web.dev notes JS grows with the app and hurts INP, so a tight JS budget is the lever.
Split on route and heavy widgets with dynamic import so first load only ships what the landing screen needs. Prefetch likely next routes.
Crawlers and share-card bots may not run JavaScript, so public pages usually need prerendering or SSR. Keep pure CSR for behind-login areas.

instead.why: Public content pages that need fast first paint and SEO without a render server
Dynamic pages where users should see content before all JS has loaded

breaks.d: Large bundle plus a data waterfall delays the first meaningful paint.
breaks.see: High LCP, long white screen, poor INP in field data
breaks.fix: Route-level code splitting, a JS budget, skeleton shell, start fetches early

breaks.d: Old HTML points at hashed chunks that a new deploy deleted.
breaks.fix: Serve index.html with no-cache, keep old chunks for a while, handle the preload error by reloading (Vite emits vite:preloadError)

breaks.d: Bots that do not run JS get only the shell.
breaks.see: Missing titles and descriptions in search or link previews
breaks.fix: Prerender or SSR public routes; keep CSR for private screens

say: For a logged-in dashboard I would choose a client-rendered SPA: static hosting on a CDN, and after the first load every navigation is instant.
The cost is the first load - HTML, then JS, then data - so I enforce a JavaScript budget, split by route and start data fetches at the router level to avoid a waterfall.
For any public, SEO-sensitive page I would not rely on CSR alone; I would prerender or server-render it and keep the SPA for the app behind login.

followups.q: How do you improve first load of an SPA?
followups.a: Smaller critical bundle via route splitting and tree shaking, preload the route chunk and its data early, ship a lightweight shell or skeleton, cache hashed assets for a long time, and measure LCP and INP in the field.

followups.q: Why does the same URL work after refresh on /settings?
followups.a: The host must rewrite unknown paths to index.html (history fallback) so the client router can read the URL and render the right view.

today: Pure SPAs are now usually a deliberate choice for authenticated apps. Frameworks such as Next.js can start as a strict SPA or static export and later add Server Components and Server Actions, and Vite builds target Baseline widely available browsers by default.

check.q: What does the server return for /dashboard in a pure CSR SPA?
check.a: The same small index.html shell as for every route
d: A fully rendered HTML page for that route
check.why: The router in the browser reads the URL and renders the view; the host just falls back to index.html.

check.q: Which is the main cost of CSR?
check.a: Content waits for JS download and execution, then data fetch
d: It needs a database on every request
check.why: First paint depends on the bundle and a fetch waterfall, so JS size drives load and INP.

check.q: When is CSR a good fit?
check.a: Logged-in tools where SEO does not matter
d: Public blog posts needing search ranking
Pages that must work with JavaScript off
check.why: Behind a login there is no crawler, and app-like navigation is the benefit.
